children.note: Every bit of state power is the people's — Kenyans own it — and may only be used the way this Constitution allows. The people use it themselves (for example in a referendum) or through the leaders they elect.

children.topic: Clause 1: power belongs to the people
children.note: All sovereign power is the people's, and it may be exercised only as the Constitution says.

manas.q: Who holds sovereign power in Kenya, and on what condition?

children.note: The people act directly (a referendum, a petition) or through the representatives they elect democratically.

children.topic: Clause 3: delegated to three kinds of State organ
children.note: The people lend their power to Parliament and the county assemblies, the national and county executives, and the Judiciary and independent tribunals. Each must act within the Constitution.

manas.q: To which State organs is sovereign power delegated?

children.note: Parliament (National Assembly and Senate) and the 47 county assemblies make law.
The national executive (President, Cabinet) and the county executives (governors) carry out the law.
Courts and independent tribunals decide disputes and check the other two.
Sovereign power is exercised at the national level and at the county level.

manas.q: At which two levels is sovereign power exercised?

children.note: The Constitution is the highest law and binds every person and every State organ at both levels of government. Anything that clashes with it is void, as far as the clash goes.
The Constitution sits above all other law and binds every person and every State organ, national and county.

manas.q: Whom does the Constitution bind?

children.topic: Clause 2: no State authority outside it
children.note: Nobody may claim or use State authority unless the Constitution authorises it.

children.topic: Clause 3: cannot be challenged in court
children.note: No court or State organ may question whether the Constitution itself is valid or legal.
A law of any kind, customary law included, that contradicts the Constitution is void as far as the contradiction goes; an act done against the Constitution is invalid.

manas.q: What happens to a law that conflicts with the Constitution?

children.note: Only the clashing part dies; the rest of the Act survives. Courts usually sever the bad section.
A custom (for example on inheritance) that discriminates contrary to Article 27 is void on that point.
A county by-law that bans all demonstrations would clash with Article 37 and be void to that extent.
The general rules of international law are part of Kenyan law.

children.topic: Clause 6: ratified treaties are Kenyan law
children.note: A treaty or convention that Kenya has ratified becomes Kenyan law by force of the Constitution itself.

manas.q: When does a treaty become part of Kenyan law?

children.note: Everyone has a duty to respect, uphold and defend the Constitution. Trying to set up a government in any other way than the Constitution allows is unlawful.

children.topic: Clause 1: a duty on every person
children.note: Respecting, upholding and defending the Constitution is an obligation of every person, not only officials.

manas.q: Who has the duty to defend the Constitution?

children.note: Any attempt to establish a government outside the Constitution (for example a coup) is unlawful.
Kenyan decisions read on Kenya Law (new.kenyalaw.org) that turned on this chapter. One line each; open the link for the judgment.

children.topic: AG v Ndii (BBI case), Supreme Court 2022
children.note: The Supreme Court held that the "basic structure" doctrine (an unamendable core) does not apply in Kenya, and that the President cannot start a constitutional amendment through the popular-initiative route. The Constitution of Kenya (Amendment) Bill 2020 was therefore unconstitutional. Shows how Article 1 sovereignty is exercised only through the Constitution's own amendment rules (Chapter 16).

manas.q: What did the Supreme Court decide about the basic structure doctrine in the BBI case (2022)?

children.note: Kenya is a sovereign Republic. It is a multi-party democratic State built on the national values in Article 10.
Kenya answers to no outside power; it is a republic, not a monarchy.
The State is a multi-party democracy founded on the Article 10 values and principles of governance.

manas.q: What kind of State does Article 4 say Kenya is?

children.note: Kenya is the land and territorial waters it had on the effective date (27 August 2010), plus any territory added later by an Act of Parliament.

manas.q: How can Kenya's territory be extended?

children.topic: Art. 6 · Devolution and access to services
children.note: Kenya is divided into the counties listed in the First Schedule. National and county governments are distinct but interdependent and must consult and cooperate; national organs must make their services reasonably available across the country.
The territory is divided into the counties named in the First Schedule (47 counties).

manas.q: Where are the counties listed?

children.note: The two levels of government are separate but depend on each other, and must relate by consultation and cooperation.

manas.q: How must national and county governments relate to each other?

children.note: A national State organ must make its services reasonably reachable in every part of Kenya, as far as the nature of the service allows.

children.topic: Art. 7 · National, official and other languages
children.note: Kiswahili is the national language; Kiswahili and English are the official languages. The State must protect language diversity and promote indigenous languages, plus Kenyan Sign Language, Braille and other accessible formats.
Kiswahili is the national language of the Republic.

manas.q: What is Kenya's national language?

children.note: Kiswahili and English are the official languages.

manas.q: Name the two official languages.

children.note: The State must promote and protect language diversity, and develop indigenous languages, as well as Kenyan Sign Language, Braille and other formats that persons with disabilities can use.
There is no State religion. Kenya is a secular State in the sense that no faith is official.

manas.q: Does Kenya have a State religion?

children.topic: Art. 9 · National symbols and national days
children.note: The national symbols are the flag, the anthem, the coat of arms and the public seal (set out in the Second Schedule). The national days are Madaraka Day (1 June), Mashujaa Day (20 October) and Jamhuri Day (12 December), each a public holiday.
The national flag, national anthem, coat of arms and public seal, described in the Second Schedule.

manas.q: Name the four national symbols.

children.note: Madaraka Day 1 June, Mashujaa Day 20 October, Jamhuri Day 12 December.

manas.q: Which date is Mashujaa Day?

children.note: Marks internal self-rule in 1963.
Honours the heroes of the freedom struggle (formerly Kenyatta Day).
Marks independence (1963) and the Republic (1964).
Each national day is a public holiday; Parliament may create other public holidays by legislation.

children.topic: Art. 10 · National values and principles of governance
children.note: These values bind every State organ, State officer, public officer and every person whenever they apply or interpret the Constitution or any law, or make or carry out public policy. They include patriotism, devolution, the rule of law, democracy, public participation, human dignity, equity, inclusiveness, good governance, integrity, transparency, accountability and sustainable development.
They apply whenever anyone applies or interprets the Constitution or a law, enacts a law, or makes or implements public policy decisions.

manas.q: When do the Article 10 values bind a public officer?

children.note: State organs, State officers and public officers, and in fact all persons.
Applying or interpreting the Constitution; enacting, applying or interpreting any law; making or implementing public policy.
Patriotism and national unity; sharing power and devolving it; the rule of law; democracy; participation of the people.

manas.q: Name three Article 10(2)(a) values.

children.note: Human dignity and equity; social justice; inclusiveness and equality; human rights; non-discrimination; protection of the marginalised.
Good governance, integrity, transparency and accountability.
Development that does not rob future generations.
Public participation and the rule of law are often argued from Article 10; the Supreme Court in the BBI case (2022) discussed IEBC duties under Article 10(2).

Culture is recognised as the foundation of the nation. The State must promote all forms of cultural expression, indigenous science and technology, and the people's intellectual property; Parliament must legislate for royalties to communities and for protection of indigenous seeds and plant varieties.
The Constitution treats culture as the nation's foundation and the sum of Kenyan civilisation.
Literature, the arts, traditional celebrations, science, media, libraries and heritage; indigenous technologies; the intellectual property rights of Kenyans.
Compensation or royalties for communities whose culture is used, and protection of communities' ownership of their indigenous seeds and plant varieties.

manas.q: What must Parliament legislate on under Article 11(3)?

nodeData.note: Who is a Kenyan citizen, by birth or registration; passports and identity documents; dual citizenship; when citizenship by registration can be revoked; the laws Parliament must pass. Own-words notes linked to the official text. A study aid, not legal advice. Search words: Katiba, Constitution of Kenya 2010, Article, Ibara, sheria kuu.

children.note: A citizen enjoys the rights, the privileges and the benefits of citizenship (within the Constitution's limits) and is entitled to a Kenyan passport and State identity documents. These can be denied, suspended or taken away only under an Act of Parliament that meets the Article 24 limitation test.
Rights of citizenship, a passport, and any registration or identity document the State issues to citizens.

manas.q: What documents is every citizen entitled to?

children.note: Only under an Act of Parliament, and only one that satisfies the Article 24 criteria for limiting rights.

children.topic: Art. 13 · Retention and acquisition of citizenship
children.note: Anyone who was a citizen just before the effective date keeps that status. Citizenship is acquired by birth or by registration, and marriage or divorce does not end it.
People who were citizens before 27 August 2010 remain citizens with the same status.
Birth or registration.

manas.q: What are the two ways to acquire Kenyan citizenship?

children.topic: Clause 3: marriage does not change it
children.note: Citizenship is not lost by marrying or by the end of a marriage.

manas.q: Does divorce affect citizenship?

children.note: Someone is a citizen by birth when, on their day of birth, either parent is a citizen, whether born in Kenya or abroad. A child found in Kenya who appears under eight with unknown parents is presumed a citizen by birth, and a citizen by birth who lost citizenship by taking another may regain it on application.
Mother or father being a citizen on the day of birth is enough; place of birth does not matter.

manas.q: Is a child born abroad to a Kenyan mother a citizen by birth?

children.note: Before 2010 descent through the mother was restricted; the 2010 text treats both parents alike.

children.topic: Born in Kenya to foreign parents
children.note: Birth on Kenyan soil alone does not make a citizen; a parent must be a citizen.
The same rule covers people born before the effective date, if either parent is or was a citizen.

children.topic: Clause 3: Parliament may limit descent abroad
children.note: Parliament may pass a law limiting the rule for descendants of Kenyans born outside Kenya.
A child found in Kenya, apparently under eight, with unknown parents and nationality, is presumed a citizen by birth.

manas.q: What is the age limit in the foundling rule?

children.note: A citizen by birth who lost citizenship by acquiring another country's may regain Kenyan citizenship on application.

A spouse of a citizen married for at least seven years is entitled to register; a lawful resident of seven continuous years may apply under conditions set by Parliament; a child adopted by a citizen is entitled to register. Parliament sets conditions for granting citizenship to foreigners.
Married to a citizen for at least seven years: entitled on application.

manas.q: How long must a spouse be married to a citizen before registering?

children.note: Lawfully resident for a continuous seven years and meeting the Act's conditions: may apply.
A non-citizen child whom a citizen adopts has the right, on application, to be registered.
Parliament must legislate the conditions for granting citizenship to citizens of other countries.
Periods completed before, after or across the effective date all count toward the requirements.
Taking another country's citizenship does not cost a citizen by birth their Kenyan citizenship.

manas.q: Can a Kenyan by birth hold a second nationality?

children.note: Citizenship by registration can be revoked for fraud or concealment, helping an enemy in wartime, a prison sentence of three years or more within five years of registration, or conviction for treason or an offence carrying at least seven years. A presumed foundling's citizenship can be revoked if the facts (fraud, foreign nationality, age over eight) come out.
Four grounds: fraud or concealment; aiding an enemy during a war; conviction and sentence of 3+ years within 5 years of registration; conviction for treason or an offence punishable by 7+ years.

manas.q: Name two grounds for revoking citizenship by registration.

children.note: Citizenship obtained by fraud, false representation or hiding a material fact.
Trading or communicating with an enemy, or running a business that knowingly helped one, during a war Kenya fought.
Convicted within five years of registration and sentenced to three years or more.
Conviction for treason, or for an offence that carries at least seven years.
Revocable if obtained by fraud, if the person turns out to be a citizen of another country, or if they were over eight when found.
Article 17 speaks only of citizenship by registration and of presumed foundlings; it gives no ground for revoking citizenship by birth.

manas.q: Can citizenship by birth be revoked under Article 17?

children.note: Parliament must pass laws on how to become a citizen, entry and residence, permanent residents, voluntary renunciation, revocation procedures, and the duties and rights of citizens.
Procedures to become a citizen; entry and residence; permanent residence; giving up citizenship; revocation procedure; duties and rights of citizens.
The Act Parliament passed under this Article is the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act; check its current text on new.kenyalaw.org before relying on any detail (checked 6 Nov 2026).

children.topic: Part 1 · How the Bill of Rights works (19–25)
children.note: Purpose, who it binds, State duties, going to court, remedies, the limitation test and the four absolute rights.

The Bill of Rights is a core part of Kenya's democracy and the frame for social, economic and cultural policy. Rights belong to each person and are not a gift of the State; the list is not closed, and rights may be limited only as the Constitution allows.
The Bill of Rights is part of the democratic State and the frame within which social, economic and cultural policies are made.
To preserve the dignity of people and of communities, to promote social justice and to let everyone realise their potential.

children.topic: Clause 3: not granted by the State
children.note: Rights belong to each individual; other rights recognised by law are not excluded; limits only as the Constitution contemplates.

manas.q: Does the State grant the rights in the Bill of Rights?

children.topic: Art. 20 · Application of Bill of Rights
children.note: The Bill of Rights governs all law and binds every State organ and every person, so private actors are covered too. Courts must develop the law and prefer the reading that best enforces a right; when the State pleads lack of resources for an Article 43 right, it must prove it.
All law, all State organs and all persons, including private individuals and companies.

manas.q: Does the Bill of Rights bind private persons?

children.note: Each person enjoys each right to the greatest extent consistent with its nature.

children.topic: Clause 3: courts must develop the law
children.note: Where the law fails to give effect to a right, a court must develop it and adopt the interpretation that most favours enforcing the right.
The values of an open, democratic society built on dignity, on equality and equity, and on freedom; the spirit, purpose and objects of the Bill of Rights.

The State must show the resources are unavailable; it must prioritise the widest enjoyment of the right with regard to vulnerable groups; a court may not overturn an allocation decision only because it would have decided differently.

manas.q: Who bears the burden when the State says it lacks resources for a social right?

children.topic: Art. 21 · Implementation of rights and fundamental freedoms
children.note: The State and every State organ must observe, respect, protect, promote and fulfil all rights. It must take measures for the progressive realisation of the Article 43 social-economic rights, address the needs of vulnerable groups, and legislate to meet Kenya's international human-rights obligations.
Observe, respect, protect, promote and fulfil.

manas.q: Name the five verbs in Article 21(1).

children.note: Legislative, policy and other measures, including standards, to progressively achieve the Article 43 rights.
Women; older people; persons with disabilities; children; youth; minority and marginalised communities; particular ethnic, religious or cultural communities.
The State must enact and implement laws to fulfil its international human-rights obligations.

children.topic: Art. 22 · Enforcement of Bill of Rights
children.note: Anyone may go to court claiming a right has been denied, violated, infringed or threatened. Standing is wide (on behalf of others, for a group, in the public interest, or by an association), and the Chief Justice's rules must keep formalities minimal with no filing fee.
Every person may institute proceedings over a denied, violated, infringed or threatened right.
A person acting for someone who cannot act, for a group or class, in the public interest, or an association for its members.

manas.q: Who may bring a Bill of Rights case besides the victim?

children.note: Must facilitate standing, keep formalities minimal (informal documents allowed), charge no fee, avoid procedural technicalities, and allow friends of the court.

manas.q: May a court fee be charged for starting an Article 22 case?

children.topic: Clause 4: no rules, still a right
children.note: Missing rules do not stop anyone from filing and being heard.

children.topic: Art. 23 · Authority of courts to uphold and enforce the Bill of Rights
children.note: The High Court hears claims for redress of rights violations (per Article 165), and Parliament must give subordinate courts original jurisdiction in suitable cases. Relief can include declarations, injunctions, conservatory orders, invalidating a law, compensation and judicial review.
The High Court decides claims for redress when a right is denied, violated, infringed or threatened.

manas.q: Which court has jurisdiction over Bill of Rights claims?

children.note: Parliament must legislate to let magistrates' courts hear appropriate rights cases.
Declaration of rights; injunction; conservatory order; declaration that a law is invalid (if not justified under Article 24); compensation; judicial review.

manas.q: Name four remedies a court may grant under Article 23(3).

children.topic: Art. 24 · Limitation of rights and fundamental freedoms
children.note: A right may be limited only by law, and only as far as is reasonable and can be justified in an open, democratic society, weighing five factors. Whoever limits the right must prove the test is met; equality bends only as strictly necessary for Kadhis' courts, and some rights may be limited for soldiers and police.
By law; reasonable; justifiable in an open, democratic society built on dignity, equality and freedom.

manas.q: State the Article 24(1) limitation test in one line.

children.note: Nature of the right; importance of the purpose; nature and extent of the limitation; protecting others' rights; whether a less restrictive means would do.

manas.q: What are the five factors in Article 24(1)?

children.topic: Clause 2: the law must say so
children.note: A post-2010 law limiting a right must expressly state the intention and the extent; it must be clear and specific; it may never cut into the core of a right.
The State or person seeking to justify the limit must prove the requirements are met.

manas.q: Who must prove that a limitation is justified?

children.note: Equality rules give way only as strictly necessary for Muslim law before Kadhis' courts, for Muslims, in personal status, marriage, divorce and inheritance.
Laws may limit privacy, association, assembly, labour relations, social-economic rights and arrested-persons rights for members of the Kenya Defence Forces and the National Police Service.

manas.q: Which rights may be limited for KDF and police members?

children.topic: Art. 25 · Rights that may not be limited
children.note: Four rights can never be limited: freedom from torture and from cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment; freedom from slavery or servitude; a fair trial; and habeas corpus.
No torture or cruel treatment; no slavery or servitude; fair trial; habeas corpus.

manas.q: Which four rights are absolute under Article 25?

children.note: A court order that a detained person be produced so the court can test whether the detention is lawful.

Life, equality, dignity, liberty, privacy, belief, expression, media, information, association, assembly, politics, movement, property, labour, environment, social rights, culture, family, consumers, administration, justice, arrest, fair trial, detention.

Everyone has the right to life, which the Constitution says begins at conception. Life may not be taken intentionally except as authorised by the Constitution or written law, and abortion is not permitted unless a trained health professional judges that emergency treatment is needed or the mother's life or health is in danger, or another written law permits it.
The Constitution states that a person's life begins at conception.
Only to the extent the Constitution or another written law authorises.
Not permitted unless, in a trained health professional's opinion, emergency treatment is needed or the mother's life or health is at risk, or another written law permits.

manas.q: When does Article 26(4) allow abortion?

children.topic: Art. 27 · Equality and freedom from discrimination
children.note: Everyone is equal before the law with equal protection and benefit of it, and women and men have equal rights. Neither the State nor anyone else may discriminate on grounds such as race, sex, pregnancy, health status, ethnicity, age, disability, religion, dress or birth; the State must take affirmative action and keep any elective or appointive body below two-thirds of one gender.
Equal protection by the law and equal benefit from it; full enjoyment of all rights; equal treatment and opportunities for women and men.

Race; sex; pregnancy; marital or health status; ethnicity or social origin; skin colour; age; disability; religion, conscience or belief; culture, dress or language; birth. "Including" means the list is open.

manas.q: Is the list of discrimination grounds in Article 27(4) closed?

children.note: A person may not discriminate against another on those grounds either.
The State must take measures, including affirmative action, to redress past discrimination, with benefits based on genuine need.
The State must legislate and act so that at most two-thirds of any elective or appointive body's members are of one gender.

manas.q: What is the two-thirds gender rule?

children.note: The Supreme Court (majority) advised that the two-thirds gender principle for the National Assembly and Senate is to be realised progressively, with legislation to be in place by 27 August 2015, not at the March 2013 election. Chief Justice Mutunga dissented.

manas.q: Did the Supreme Court in 2012 say the two-thirds rule applied immediately to Parliament?

children.note: Dignity is inherent in every person, who has the right to have it respected and protected.

manas.q: What does Article 28 protect?

children.topic: Art. 29 · Freedom and security of the person
children.note: No one may be deprived of freedom arbitrarily, detained without trial (except in an emergency under Article 58), subjected to violence from public or private sources, tortured physically or psychologically, given corporal punishment, or treated in a cruel, inhuman or degrading way.

children.topic: (a)–(b): liberty and no detention without trial
children.note: No arbitrary loss of freedom; detention without trial only in a state of emergency, subject to Article 58.
Protection from violence by the State and by private persons alike, which is why domestic violence engages this Article.

manas.q: Does Article 29 cover violence by private persons?

children.note: No torture, physical or psychological; no corporal punishment; no treatment or punishment that is cruel, inhuman or degrading.

manas.q: Is corporal punishment allowed under Article 29?

children.topic: Art. 30 · Slavery, servitude and forced labour
children.note: Nobody may be held in slavery or servitude, and nobody may be required to perform forced labour.

manas.q: Which Article bans forced labour?

children.note: Everyone has the right to privacy: no search of their person, home or property, no seizure of possessions, no unnecessary demands for or disclosure of family or private information, and no interference with their communications.
Search of person, home or property; seizure of possessions; family or private information; privacy of communications.

manas.q: Name the four strands of the right to privacy.

children.note: The Data Protection Act 2019 gives effect to Article 31(c) and (d); check the current Act on new.kenyalaw.org (checked 6 Nov 2026).

children.topic: Art. 32 · Freedom of conscience, religion, belief and opinion
children.note: Everyone may hold any belief and practise any religion, alone or with others, in public or private, including observing a day of worship. Nobody may be denied access to an institution, job or facility because of their belief, or forced to act against it.
Freedom of conscience, of religion, of thought, belief and opinion; freedom to manifest it through worship, practice, teaching or observance.
No denial of access to institutions, employment, facilities or rights because of belief or religion.

manas.q: Can a school exclude a learner because of their religion?

children.note: A person may not be compelled to act against their belief or religion.

Everyone may seek, receive and share information and ideas, create art and do academic and scientific work freely. The right does not cover propaganda for war, incitement to violence, hate speech or advocacy of hatred that incites ethnically or discriminates, and everyone must respect other people's rights and reputation.
Seeking, receiving or imparting information or ideas; artistic creativity; academic freedom and scientific research.
Propaganda for war; incitement to violence; hate speech; advocacy of hatred that is ethnic incitement or vilification, or rests on an Article 27(4) ground.

manas.q: Name the four kinds of expression Article 33 does not protect.

children.note: The right is exercised with respect for the rights and reputation of others (the constitutional hook for defamation law).

Media freedom and independence are guaranteed (within the Article 33(2) limits). The State may not control or interfere with broadcasters or publishers or punish opinions; licensing must be independent and only to manage the airwaves; State media must be impartial and editorially independent; Parliament must create an independent body to set media standards.
No control over broadcasting or publishing, and no penalty for an opinion or content.

manas.q: May the State penalise a publisher for the content of a broadcast?

children.note: Free to set up, subject only to licensing needed to regulate the airwaves and independent of government, political and commercial control.
Editorially independent, impartial, and fair to divergent and dissenting views.
Parliament must create a body, independent of government and commercial interests, to set and enforce media standards.

Every citizen may access information held by the State, and information held by anyone else that is needed to exercise or protect a right. Everyone may have untrue or misleading information about them corrected or deleted, and the State must publish important information affecting the nation.
Information held by the State; and information held by another person if required to exercise or protect a right.

manas.q: Who holds the Article 35(1) right of access to information?

children.note: Any person may demand that untrue or misleading information about them be corrected or deleted.
The State must publish and publicise important information affecting the nation.

Everyone may form, join or take part in any association and nobody may be forced to join one. A registration law may not withhold or withdraw registration unreasonably and must give a fair hearing before cancellation.
Freedom to form, join or participate; freedom not to be compelled to join.

manas.q: Can a person be compelled to join an association?

children.note: No unreasonable refusal or withdrawal of registration; fair hearing before cancellation.

children.topic: Art. 37 · Assembly, demonstration, picketing and petition
children.note: Everyone may, peacefully and unarmed, assemble, demonstrate, picket and present petitions to public authorities.

manas.q: What two conditions does Article 37 put on the right to demonstrate?

children.note: Every citizen may make political choices: form, join, recruit for or campaign for a party or cause. Citizens are entitled to elections that are free, fair and regular, by universal suffrage, and every adult citizen may register as a voter, vote by secret ballot, and stand for and hold office.
Form or help form a party; participate in or recruit for a party; campaign for a party or cause.
By universal suffrage, freely expressing the electors' will, for public bodies and for party offices.

manas.q: What does Article 38(2) guarantee about elections?

children.note: To be registered as a voter; to vote (secret ballot) at any election or referendum; to be a candidate and hold office if elected.

manas.q: At what status does the right to vote attach?

children.topic: Art. 39 · Freedom of movement and residence
children.note: Everyone may move freely and leave Kenya; every citizen may enter, remain in and live anywhere in Kenya.
Movement and the right to leave are for every person; the right to enter, remain and reside anywhere is for citizens.

manas.q: Who has the right to enter and remain in Kenya under Article 39?

children.topic: Art. 40 · Protection of right to property
children.note: Everyone may acquire and own property of any kind anywhere in Kenya (subject to Article 65 on land ownership by non-citizens). The State may take property only through Chapter Five land processes or for a public purpose with prompt, full and just compensation and access to court; intellectual property is protected and unlawfully acquired property is not.
Individually or with others, property of any description, in any part of Kenya, subject to Article 65.
Parliament may not pass a law allowing arbitrary deprivation or restricting property rights on an Article 27(4) ground.
Only under Chapter Five land rules, or for a public purpose under an Act that requires just compensation, paid promptly and in full, and allows access to court.

manas.q: What must the State pay when it compulsorily acquires property?

children.note: Compensation may be provided for good-faith occupants of acquired land who hold no title.
The State protects intellectual property; the Article does not protect property found to have been unlawfully acquired.

manas.q: Does Article 40 protect property that was unlawfully acquired?

children.note: Everyone is entitled to fair labour practices. Workers have the right to fair pay, reasonable conditions, joining a trade union and striking; employers may form organisations; unions and employers' organisations run their own affairs and may federate; all may bargain collectively.
Fair remuneration; reasonable working conditions; trade-union membership and activity; the right to strike.

manas.q: Name the four rights of every worker in Article 41(2).

children.note: Employers may form and join employers' organisations; unions and employers' organisations control their administration, organise and federate.
Trade unions, employers' organisations and employers may bargain collectively.

Everyone is entitled to a clean, healthy environment, protected for present and future generations through the measures in Article 69, and to have the environmental obligations in Article 70 fulfilled.

manas.q: Which Articles does Article 42 point to for environmental duties and enforcement?

children.note: Everyone is entitled to the best attainable standard of health (including reproductive health care), adequate housing and sanitation, freedom from hunger and adequate food, clean and safe water, social security and education. Nobody may be denied emergency medical treatment, and the State must provide social security to those who cannot support themselves.
Health; housing and sanitation; food; water; social security; education.

manas.q: List the six Article 43 rights.

children.note: No person may be denied emergency medical treatment.

manas.q: Can a hospital turn away an emergency patient?

children.note: The State must provide appropriate social security to people who cannot support themselves or their dependants.
Progressively (Article 21(2)); the State must prove lack of resources (Article 20(5)).

Everyone may use the language and join the cultural life of their choice, and may enjoy their culture and form cultural and linguistic associations with others in their community. Nobody may force anyone else to perform, observe or undergo a cultural practice or rite.
The constitutional basis for banning forced initiation or similar practices.

manas.q: May a person be compelled to undergo a cultural rite?

children.note: The family is society's natural and fundamental unit and is protected by the State. Every adult may marry someone of the opposite sex, by free consent; spouses have equal rights at, during and at the end of marriage; Parliament must recognise marriages and family-law systems under traditions and religions, as far as they fit the Constitution.
Adults, opposite sex, free consent of both parties.

manas.q: What three elements does Article 45(2) require for a marriage?

children.note: Equal rights at the time of marriage, during it and at its dissolution.
Parliament recognises traditional, religious and personal-law marriages and systems, so far as consistent with the Constitution.

Consumers are entitled to goods and to services of reasonable quality, to the information needed to benefit from them, to protection of their health, safety and economic interests, and to compensation for defects. Parliament must legislate on consumer protection and honest advertising, and the Article covers public and private providers.
Quality; information; protection of health, safety and economic interests; compensation for loss from defects.

manas.q: Name the four consumer rights.

children.note: Applies to goods and services from public entities and private persons alike.

Everyone is entitled to administrative action that is quick, efficient, lawful, reasonable and procedurally fair, and to written reasons when their rights are adversely affected. Parliament must let a court or independent tribunal review administrative action.
Expeditious, efficient, lawful, reasonable, procedurally fair.

manas.q: What five qualities must administrative action have?

children.note: A person whose right is or may be adversely affected has the right to written reasons.
Legislation must allow review by a court or an independent, impartial tribunal (the Fair Administrative Action Act; check the current text).
The State must ensure access to justice for all, and any fee must be reasonable and must not block access.

manas.q: What does Article 48 say about court fees?

children.note: An arrested person must be told promptly why, may stay silent, may contact an advocate, may not be forced to confess, is held apart from convicts, goes to court within 24 hours, and is then charged or released, with bail on reasonable terms unless there are compelling reasons. Nobody may be remanded for an offence punishable only by a fine or up to six months in prison.
Reason for arrest, the right to remain silent and the consequences of not doing so, in a language the person understands.
Contact an advocate and others whose help is needed; no compelled confession; held separately from sentenced prisoners.
To court as soon as reasonably possible and not later than 24 hours, or by the close of the next court day if the 24 hours run out outside court hours.

manas.q: Within how long must an arrested person be brought to court?

children.note: At first appearance: charged, told why detention continues, or released; bail or bond on reasonable conditions unless compelling reasons exist.

manas.q: When may bail be refused under Article 49(1)(h)?

children.note: No remand in custody where the offence carries only a fine or at most six months' imprisonment.

manas.q: Can a person be remanded for an offence punishable by a fine only?

children.note: Every dispute that law can resolve must get a fair and public hearing before an independent court or tribunal. An accused person has a long list of fair-trial rights, from the presumption of innocence and disclosure of evidence to a free interpreter, no double jeopardy, the lighter of changed sentences and a right of appeal; evidence obtained by violating rights is excluded if it would make the trial unfair.
Before a court, or another tribunal or body that is independent and impartial.

Presumed innocent; told the charge; time and facilities to prepare; public trial; no unreasonable delay; present at trial; choose an advocate; a State-paid advocate if substantial injustice would otherwise result.

manas.q: When must the State assign an advocate at its expense?

children.note: Silence; advance disclosure of prosecution evidence; adduce and challenge evidence; no self-incrimination; free interpreter; no retroactive offences; no double jeopardy; least severe of changed punishments; appeal or review.

manas.q: What does Article 50(2)(o) protect against?

children.note: Evidence obtained in breach of a right is excluded if admitting it would make the trial unfair or harm the administration of justice.

manas.q: When is unlawfully obtained evidence excluded?

children.note: Right to the trial record; a convicted person may ask the High Court to order a new trial when appeals are exhausted and new, compelling evidence appears.
Courts may allow intermediaries; the public may be excluded to protect witnesses, morality, order or security; Parliament must legislate for victims' rights.
The right to a fair trial is one of the four Article 25 rights that may never be limited.

children.topic: Art. 51 · Rights of persons detained, held in custody or imprisoned
children.note: A detained or imprisoned person keeps every right in the Bill of Rights except those clearly incompatible with being detained. They may petition for habeas corpus, and Parliament must legislate for humane treatment in line with international human-rights instruments.
All rights remain except those clearly incompatible with detention.

manas.q: Does a prisoner lose the right to vote automatically?

children.note: A detained person may ask the court for habeas corpus (absolute under Article 25).
Children, persons with disabilities, youth, minorities and marginalised groups, older members of society.
Part 3 spells out how certain rights apply to particular groups so there is more certainty; it never limits or qualifies any right.

manas.q: Does Part 3 of the Bill of Rights limit any right?

children.note: Every child has the right to a name and nationality, free and compulsory basic education, basic nutrition, shelter and health care, protection from abuse, neglect, harmful practices, violence and exploitative labour, and care from both parents whether married or not. Detention is a last resort, for the shortest time, apart from adults; the child's best interests are paramount in every matter.
Name and nationality from birth; free and compulsory basic education; basic nutrition, shelter and health care.

manas.q: Is basic education free and compulsory under Article 53?

children.note: Protection from abuse, neglect, harmful cultural practices, violence, inhuman treatment and hazardous labour; equal parental responsibility of mother and father, married or not.

manas.q: Do unmarried fathers share responsibility for a child under Article 53?

children.note: Only as a last resort, for the shortest appropriate time, separate from adults, with regard to sex and age.
The child's best interests come first in every matter concerning the child.

manas.q: What is the paramount consideration in matters concerning a child?

children.note: A person with a disability is entitled to dignity and respectful address, integrated education, reasonable access to places, transport and information, Sign language or Braille, and assistive materials and devices. The State must progressively ensure at least five per cent of members of elective and appointive public bodies are persons with disabilities.
Dignity; integrated education; access to places, transport and information; Sign language, Braille, other communication; assistive materials and devices.

manas.q: Name three entitlements under Article 54(1).

children.note: Progressive implementation of at least 5% representation in elective and appointive bodies.

manas.q: What percentage does Article 54(2) set?

children.note: The State must take measures, including affirmative action, so that young people get relevant education and training, can associate, be represented and take part in political, social and economic life, find employment, and are shielded from harmful cultural practices and from exploitation.

manas.q: Name two things the State must do for the youth under Article 55.

children.note: The State must run affirmative-action programmes so minorities and marginalised groups take part in governance, get special opportunities in education, the economy and employment, develop their cultures and languages, and get reasonable access to water, to health services and to infrastructure.

manas.q: Which services does Article 56(e) name for marginalised groups?

children.note: The State must ensure older persons can participate fully in society, pursue personal development, live in dignity free from abuse, and receive reasonable care from family and the State.

manas.q: Who must care for older persons under Article 57(d)?

children.note: When an emergency may be declared, for how long, and what it may not do.

An emergency can be declared only through Article 132(4)(d), only for war, invasion, insurrection, disorder, natural disaster or other public emergency, and only when necessary. It lasts at most 14 days unless the National Assembly extends it, the Supreme Court may test its validity, and rights may be limited only as strictly required.
Only under Article 132(4)(d) (the President), only for the listed threats, and only if necessary.

manas.q: Who declares a state of emergency, and under which Article?

children.note: Effective only prospectively and for at most fourteen days unless the National Assembly extends it.

manas.q: How long does a declaration last without extension?

children.note: After public debate, two months at a time; first extension needs two-thirds of all MPs, later ones three-quarters.

manas.q: What majority is needed for a second extension?

children.note: The Supreme Court may decide whether a declaration, an extension or emergency legislation is valid.
Emergency laws limit rights only as strictly required and consistent with international law, take effect only once gazetted, and cannot indemnify the State or anyone for unlawful acts.
The Kenya National Human Rights and Equality Commission and its successors.

children.topic: Art. 59 · Kenya National Human Rights and Equality Commission
children.note: Article 59 creates the Commission to promote human rights and gender equality, monitor and investigate violations (including by security organs), handle complaints, oversee Kenya's human-rights treaty compliance and investigate maladministration. Anyone may complain to it, and Parliament may split it into two or more commissions, each with Chapter 15 status.

Promote a human-rights culture; gender equality and mainstreaming; monitor, investigate and report; receive complaints and secure redress; lead treaty compliance; investigate abuse of power and maladministration.

manas.q: Name three functions of the Commission in Article 59(2).

children.note: Every person may complain that a right has been denied, violated, infringed or threatened.

Parliament may restructure it into separate commissions, each with equivalent powers and Chapter 15 status. In practice there are now the KNCHR, the National Gender and Equality Commission and the Commission on Administrative Justice (Ombudsman); check the current Acts.

manas.q: Into which bodies was the Article 59 Commission split?
